subject: Climate & Environment
title: Heat Waves and Human Limits
description: A fast breakdown of Heat Waves and Human Limits for builders.

hook.text: The human body cools itself by sweating. When humidity is too high, that mechanism fails.

buildup.text: Wet-bulb temperature combines heat and humidity. Above 35°C wet-bulb, humans cannot survive outdoors.

discovery.text: Parts of the Persian Gulf and South Asia have already approached this lethal threshold.

twist.text: The 2003 European heat wave killed over 70,000 people — many elderly and alone.

climax.text: By 2050, heat exposure could affect 1.2 billion people annually. Air conditioning uses more energy.

punchline.text: There's a temperature above which the human body simply gives up.

quiz.question: What makes wet-bulb temperature dangerous to humans?
options: Sweat can't evaporate when humidity is too high

details.summary: Heat waves are becoming more frequent, longer, and more intense due to climate change, pushing human heat tolerance toward its physiological limits. Wet-bulb temperatures above 35 degrees Celsius would be fatal to healthy adults within hours even in shade.
details.whyItMatters: Heat is the deadliest weather hazard, killing more people than hurricanes and tornadoes combined. Climate change is making lethal heat events increasingly likely.
takeaways: Heat waves kill more people annually than any other weather event
Wet-bulb temperature above 35 degrees Celsius is unsurvivable
Regions near the Persian Gulf may regularly exceed this limit by 2100

faq.question: What is wet-bulb temperature?
faq.answer: Wet-bulb temperature combines heat and humidity into a single measure. At 35 degrees Celsius wet-bulb, the human body cannot cool itself through sweating because the air is too humid. Healthy individuals die of heat stroke within hours even at rest.

faq.question: Who is most vulnerable to heat waves?
faq.answer: Elderly people, outdoor workers, the homeless, people with chronic illnesses, and those without air conditioning are at highest risk. Urban heat islands and poverty significantly increase exposure and mortality during heat events.
